War Without Congress, Courts Without Teeth

A week of unilateral strikes on Iran, a domestic troop deployment, mass immigration raids, and a Supreme Court ruling that curbed judges' power to check it all

```markdown This was a week that began with bombs falling on Iran and ended with the Supreme Court narrowing the tools courts use to check the president. In between, National Guard troops occupied the streets of Los Angeles, a Justice Department official accused of contemplating defiance of federal judges sat for Senate questioning, and immigration enforcement expanded into new detention facilities in California and the Florida Everglades. It was a week in which institutions pushed back against executive power almost daily—and one in which, by Friday, some of their sharpest tools had been dulled.

The weekend opened with the most consequential single act of the period: President Trump ordered B-2 bombers to strike three Iranian nuclear facilities—Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan—the first American bombing of Iranian soil in decades. No vote was held in Congress, and no War Powers Resolution process was observed. Trump declared the operation a "spectacular success" even as his own officials cautioned that damage assessments were premature. Within days, that claim collided with reality: intelligence assessments began circulating that contradicted the president's account of the strikes' effectiveness, setting up a dispute that would occupy the rest of the week. It was not the first time in recent months that Trump had brushed aside his intelligence agencies. Months earlier, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard had testified that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon; Trump publicly rejected that finding, saying flatly that "my intelligence community is wrong." By week's end, Gabbard had realigned her public position with the administration's.

The same weekend, roughly 4,000 National Guard troops and 700 Marines arrived in Los Angeles to reinforce immigration raids that had begun weeks earlier, deployed over the objections of state and local officials. The military presence deepened an already volatile standoff between protesters and federal agents. In Newark, that same enforcement climate produced a striking legal confrontation: Mayor Ras Baraka was charged with trespassing at an ICE facility, and Rep. LaMonica McIver was charged with assaulting and impeding law enforcement during the same standoff. A federal magistrate later rebuked prosecutors for the haste of the Baraka charge, which was quietly dropped, but the message sent by charging a sitting mayor and a member of Congress in connection with oversight of a detention facility was not lost on observers. Amid this, a rare judicial check landed in favor of due process: a federal judge ordered the release of Palestinian rights activist Mahmoud Khalil after more than 100 days in ICE detention without charge, finding no evidence he posed a flight risk. The administration appealed immediately.

By Monday, the legal system was engaged on multiple fronts. California sued over the federalization of its National Guard, and fifteen Democratic attorneys general sued over Trump's declared "energy emergency," arguing it improperly bypassed environmental review. A federal judge in New York blocked the administration's use of the 1798 Alien Enemies Act to treat Venezuelan migrants as an "invasion," rejecting a legal theory underpinning parts of the deportation campaign. Judge Burroughs issued an injunction against the administration's attempt to bar international students from Harvard, warning of efforts to "squelch diverse viewpoints," while Judge Young ordered hundreds of terminated NIH grants restored, calling the cancellations "bereft of reasoning." Yet the same day brought a very different signal from the Supreme Court, which paused a lower court ruling requiring a "meaningful opportunity" for migrants to contest deportation to third countries where they might face torture or persecution—over the dissent of the three liberal justices. And a DOJ whistleblower, attorney Erez Reuveni, came forward alleging that Emil Bove, a senior Justice Department official and Trump's nominee for a federal appellate judgeship, had suggested the department might proceed with deportations regardless of court injunctions. Beneath these headline fights, the human cost of expanding detention was becoming visible: a 68-year-old detainee died in transit—the first such death in at least a decade—and a pregnant woman in ICE custody miscarried after days of pleading for medical care.

Tuesday brought the week's clearest signal of congressional restraint. The House voted to table articles of impeachment over the unauthorized Iran strikes, with only 79 Democrats in support—a clear demonstration of limited appetite in Congress to use its strongest check on unilateral military action. Courts, meanwhile, kept working. An appeals court ordered the government to facilitate the return of a man deported to El Salvador in violation of a prior court order, and a separate judge blocked Trump's executive order stripping collective bargaining rights from more than a million federal employees. But the conflict between the executive and the judiciary sharpened further: California formally sued over the Guard deployment, and the Justice Department, in an unusual escalation, sued the entire federal bench in Maryland over a standing order that delayed deportations pending legal challenge. Additional reporting detailed the Reuveni whistleblower letter, alleging Bove had suggested defying court orders and that Reuveni himself was fired after refusing to mislead a court. Meanwhile ICE enforcement kept expanding—arrests surging past facility capacity, reports emerging of DHS messaging encouraging citizens to report immigrants, and revelations about Stephen Miller's undisclosed financial stake in ICE contractor Palantir. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spent the day defending budget cuts that eliminated entire public health offices.

Wednesday centered on Emil Bove's Senate Judiciary Committee testimony. He denied the whistleblower's account and faced pointed questions about his role in dropping corruption charges against New York City Mayor Eric Adams and in firing prosecutors who had worked January 6 cases; Democrats accused him of weaponizing the department he was being promoted out of. The same day, following the leak of a Defense Intelligence Agency report that undercut the administration's claims about the Iran strikes' success, officials moved to restrict Congress's access to classified information—an action that drew immediate criticism from Democratic lawmakers concerned about the erosion of oversight. Health policy also shifted meaningfully: Kennedy unilaterally appointed eight new members, several known for vaccine skepticism, to the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, alarming even some Republican senators. Attorney General Pam Bondi, meanwhile, claimed ignorance of ICE agents wearing masks during raids despite video evidence to the contrary, and reports surfaced that the administration was preparing to dismiss the asylum claims of potentially hundreds of thousands of immigrants, rendering them immediately deportable. Elsewhere, the administration moved to terminate 639 more Voice of America employees as part of dismantling the U.S. Agency for Global Media, and Trump revoked security clearances from former officials Mike Pompeo, Mark Milley, and John Bolton. Still, courts issued more checks: a nationwide injunction blocked the shutdown of Job Corps centers, and Kilmar Abrego Garcia was ordered released on bail, even as officials acknowledged he could face renewed ICE custody.

Thursday's docket included a major Supreme Court ruling limiting Medicaid patients' ability to sue over their choice of healthcare provider, a 6-3 decision that will allow states to exclude Planned Parenthood from Medicaid funding. The Justice Department's lawsuit against Maryland's federal bench, filed the day before, drew wider notice as an extraordinary escalation—an executive branch agency suing an entire court as a body over its handling of deportation cases. ICE and private prison contractor CoreCivic moved to convert a shuttered prison into California's largest immigration detention facility, backed by an initial $10 million contract, over strong local opposition. In New York, the political costs of enforcement rhetoric became personal: the NYPD's hate crimes taskforce opened an investigation into death threats against Zohran Mamdani, the Democratic mayoral primary winner, amid a surge of Islamophobic rhetoric following his win, while a U.S. citizen, Andrea Velez, was mistakenly seized by federal agents during an unrelated Los Angeles raid. Away from immigration matters, the Senate parliamentarian ruled that several Republican-added provisions in the reconciliation bill, including Medicaid tax changes, could not proceed under budget rules—prompting some Republicans to call publicly for her removal—and Governor Gavin Newsom filed a $787 million defamation suit against Fox News over allegedly deceptive editing of a Trump phone call.

Friday delivered the week's structural turning point. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that federal courts likely lack authority to issue nationwide injunctions absent specific congressional authorization, limiting relief in the birthright citizenship case to named plaintiffs and leaving open whether class actions might achieve broader effect. The Court did not rule on the constitutionality of ending birthright citizenship itself—only on the scope of judicial remedy. The practical effect was immediate and far-reaching: many of the very tools lower courts had used throughout the week to block deportations, restore grants, and protect students depend on nationwide injunctions for broad effect, and that tool was now sharply constrained. The same day, in Mahmoud v. Taylor, the Court ruled that public schools must allow parents to withdraw children from lessons involving LGBTQ characters on religious grounds, with Justice Sotomayor warning in dissent that schools might respond by removing such content altogether rather than manage individual opt-outs. In Florida, the attorney general advanced a 5,000-bed migrant detention facility in the Everglades, and Governor DeSantis used emergency powers to seize the land from Miami-Dade County, prompting an environmental lawsuit. The University of Virginia's president, James Ryan, resigned as part of a settlement with the Justice Department over the university's diversity policies—federal investigative leverage translating directly into a change in university leadership. Republican Rep. Andy Ogles called publicly for the denaturalization and deportation of Zohran Mamdani, a naturalized citizen, sending a formal letter to the Attorney General. The Court also upheld a Texas law requiring age verification for pornography websites and, in Kennedy v. Braidwood, affirmed the structure of the ACA's preventive services framework while confirming the health secretary's broad authority over expert advisory panels. Outside the Russell Senate Office Building, activists were arrested protesting proposed Medicaid cuts as the Senate pushed toward a July 4 vote on the broader reconciliation bill.

Taken as a whole, the week traced a familiar but intensifying pattern in the relationship between the branches of American government: a president acting unilaterally on matters of war, intelligence, and domestic deployment; a Congress largely unwilling to invoke its formal checks even after being bypassed on a matter as consequential as military action; and a judiciary that remained active and often assertive throughout the week, blocking deportations, restoring funding, and ordering releases—only to see its principal nationwide remedy curtailed by the Supreme Court on the week's final day. Due process for migrants narrowed further, oversight of classified intelligence tightened around the executive rather than around the public, and institutions built for independent expertise—from vaccine advisory panels to university leadership to public broadcasting—came under direct political pressure. None of these developments occurred in isolation; each fed into the others, compounding across seven days into a portrait of executive power testing, and in several instances exceeding, the practical limits historically imposed by the other branches of government. ```
